senses.gloss:
granthi
(‘knot’)
------------------------------------------
‘Granthi’ means a knot. Just as a knot binds something, the three guṇas—sattva, रजस् and tamas—bind the जीव (individual सोउल्) to the world of nature. He has to untie them or cut them, to transcend them and rise to the level of the spirit.
In the tāntrik literature three granthis have been described. They are: Brahmagranthi, Viṣṇugranthi and Rudragranthi. They obstruct the upward movement of the कुण्डलिनी power.
Each of the six चक्रस् (like मूलाधार and स्वाधिष्ठान) has two granthis on either side. The Brahma-ग्रन्थि is situated between मूलाधार and स्वाधिष्ठान. The Viṣṇugranthi is situated between maṇipūra and anāhata. The Rudragranthi is situated between viśuddha and ājñā.
The कुण्डलिनी-शक्ति or power pierces these three granthis before reaching the सहस्रार, when roused by proper yogic exercises under the guidance of an expert.
See also CAKRAS and KUṆḌALINĪ.

grahayajña
(‘yajña [to appease the] ग्रहस् or प्लनेत्स्’)
------------------------------------------
Hindus have believed that the nine ग्रहस् or प्लनेत्स् like the sun, the मोओन्, or the mars have a bearing on human life. This has to be ascertained for each individual as per the details of the होरोस्चोपे. During certain periods in one’s life, some of the ग्रहस् are said to become inimical and affect the person adversely. Hence, certain rites known as ‘grahayajña’ have to be performed. They have to be done on certain days specified as good by the almanac. During such rites gifts of a cow, a conch, gold or cloth are to be given to worthy persons.

grāvastut
(‘one who praises the stone [used for crushing the सोम stalks]’)
------------------------------------------
Vedic sacrifices are of several varieties. Somayāgas, the sacrifices in which the सोम juice has to be offered as oblation, are an important type among them.
The सोम juice has to be extracted by using stone crushers called ‘grāvan’ specially meant for the purpose. The crushing or pressing (called ‘savana’) takes place three times a day. They are: prātassavana, mādhyandinasavana and tṛtīya-सवन.
The ग्रावस्तुत् is a priest who is an assistant of the होतृ priest. During the mādhyandina-सवन; he enters the havirdhānamaṇṭapa (a shed housing the two carts loaded with सोम stalks), is given a special turban to wear and then recites the grāvastotra (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.12.9-25). He is entitled for a share in the सोम juice.

grāmadevatā
(‘village deity’)
------------------------------------------
The concept of ग्रामदेवता (village deity or a tutelary deity) is as old as the human civilisation. When the early man cleared a forest area to build a human habitation he naturally felt apprehensive that the god or the deity or the spirit protecting the forest might get offended and harm him. Hence he might have started erecting some sort of monument or structure for the deity to reside, receive his worship and be pleased.
Grāmadevatās, either in their own shrines or under big trees, are seen almost all over India, especially in the rural and tribal areas. Clay images of horses and elephants are often placed in the premises of these deities. They are guardian deities situated at the entrance of the villages. Their main duty is to protect the village under their care from epidemic diseases, natural disasters and evil spirits. They are mostly मोथेर्-goddesses, aspects of पार्वती. They are worshipped by the villagers either regularly or on important occasions like the beginning of agricultural operations, for the protection of the crops, prevention of diseases as also auspicious ceremonies in the family like मर्रिअगे or birth.
Sacrificing animals like sheep, goats and buffaloes on special occasions to appease the goddess is also not uncommon.

grahaṇa
(‘[the sun or the मोओन्] being seized [by राहु]’, ‘eclipse’)
------------------------------------------
Grahaṇa or एच्लिप्से (both solar and lunar) has been given great importance in the Hindu liturgical works. That it was a natural phenomenon was known to the Hindu astronomers as can be gleaned from वराहमिहिर’s (6th cent. A. D.) Bṛhat-saṁhitā (5.8 and 13). However, the basically religious nature of the Hindus made them look with awe and wonder on such natural phenomena as reflecting God’s power and glory. Consequently they became occasions for performing religious rites.
Between the lunar and the solar eclipses, the latter has been considered as more holy and rewarding, from the standpoint of religious observances.
The observances generally prescribed are: bath before and after the एच्लिप्से, performance of worship of gods and śrāddha as also होम, giving of gifts to worthy persons, जप of गायत्री and other well-known mantras, ड़स्तिन्ग् and even giving दीक्षा or initiation.
Taking bath in holy places like कुरुक्षेत्र (near Delhi) or rivers like गोदावरी was highly commended.
Any religious act like doing जप or giving gifts was considered to confer infinitely greater results when performed during eclipses.
Certain astrological results, good or bad, were deemed to follow from eclipses depending on the नक्षत्र (constellation of the स्तर्स्) at the time of the eclipses. शान्तिस् or propitiatory rites have also been prescribed to offset the evil results.

Grantha script
------------------------------------------
One of the important factors responsible for the development of any language is its script. According to the experts in the field of paleography, the origins of writing with a definite script might be traced to the period 4000 B. C.
The Kannaḍa and the Telugu characters might have evolved around the 5th century A. D. from a South Indian edition of the ब्राह्मी script.
The Tamiḷ characters were already in use even by the 2nd century A. D. Since this script contained only the first and the last letters in each of the five vargas (like ka-varga, ca-varga, viz., ka and ṅ or ca and ñ) and did not have the letters like śa, ṣa, sa or ha, Sanskrit works could not be copied in this script. To remedy this defect, the ग्रन्थ स्च्रिप्त् seems to have been evolved. There is evidence of the use of this script in the earliest copper plate inscriptions of the पल्लवस् belonging to the 5th or the 6th century A. D. Hence the name ‘Pallava ग्रन्थ स्च्रिप्त्’ also.
Though this script was used mostly for Sanskrit writings, it seems to have gained greater currency in general use also, around the 14th century.
The Malayāḷam script is a metamorphosis of the ग्रन्थ स्च्रिप्त्.
It has been used sometimes as a script for the Tuḷu language also.
Two varieties of the ग्रन्थ स्च्रिप्त् are found: the Brāhmaṇic or the square variety and the Jaina or the round variety.
The script has 35 letters, of which five are vowels.

graves
------------------------------------------
Burial and च्रेमतिओन् of the bodies of the dead have both been an ancient practice among the Hindus. Building ग्रवेस् or sepulchral mounds over the places of बुरिअल् is common even now. However, what is not generally known is that sepulchral mounds used to be built over the charred bones of a cremated person too! After च्रेमतिओन्, the bones collected from the च्रेमतिओन् ground used to be preserved in an urn, kept either in an open ground under a tree or temporarily buried in a place, with some distinguishing marks to resurrect it later.
After a sufficiently long time, a grave used to be dug in a suitable place like a level ground full of trees and natural beauty, the bones taken out of the urn and placed in the pit in a particular order. It would then be filled with bricks, clay and earth, and a mound raised over the spot, like a monument. Of course, all this had to be done as per the procedure given in the श्रौतसूत्रस् with appropriate Vedic mantras.
This practice was not universal and went out of vouge in course of time.
See also ANTYEṢṬI, BURIAL and CREMATION.

Granth-Sāhib
(‘the Master-Book’)
------------------------------------------
Sikhism is the youngest of the world religions. It was started by गुरु Nānak (A. D. 1469-1539). It has been developed and nourished by nine more Gurus of whom the last was the illustrious गुरु Gobind Singh (A. D. 1666-1708).
The basic scripture of सिखिस्म् is the Ādi-Granth, also known as Granth Sāhib or Śrī गुरु Granth-Sāhib. It was the fifth गुरु, गुरु Arjan Dev (A. D. 1563-1606) that compiled the original edition of the Granth-Sāhib in A. D. 1604. It was later revised by गुरु Gobind Singh in A. D. 1705 by including the hymns of गुरु Tegh Bahādūr (A. D. 1621-1675) also. In A. D. 1708, he declared that there would be no more Gurus to guide the Sikhs and that the Book itself would be the गुरु and hence had to be revered as such.
The Book comprises 6000 hymns. The Gurus represented and the hymns composed by them are as follows:
Nānak: 974 hymns.
Aṅgad: 62 hymns.
Amar Das: 907 hymns.
Arjan Dev: 2,218 hymns.
Tegh Bahādūr: 115 hymns.

Compositions of other saints—called Bhagats—have also been included. For instance 61 hymns of the Maharashtrian saint नाम्देव् (A. D. 1270-1350), 39 of the mocī (shoe-maker caste) saint Raidas (15th cent. A. D.) and 226 of कबीर् (A. D. 1440-1518) form part of the Book.
The Book starts with the Japji, the famous morning prayer. This is followed by Rahiras and Kīrtan Sohila the evening and night prayers.
The gist of its teaching is that God is one and that his name is Sat or Truth. He has no birth and hence no death. He can be realised only by the grace of the गुरु. He lives in our bodies too. Repeating God’s nāma or name and remembering him through the name, is the chief mode of spiritual discipline.
See also SIKHISM.
